Marked points: \((-6,-4)\), \((-4,0)\), \((-1,4)\) (labelled), plus three unlabelled markers at the local minimum, on the rising right branch, and at the right-hand X-axis crossing. _note: BOOK DEFECT CANDIDATE — printed solution disagrees with the book's own figure. The solution states 'From graph when x = 3, y = -5 so g(3) = -5'. Fig. 6.14 was pixel-measured against its own grid: the gridlines are uniform at 44.5 px and the origin is exact, and calibrating on all three LABELLED points gives 1 square = 2 units on both axes with each labelled point accurate to within 0.15 units — measured (-6.00, -3.88), (-4.06, -0.02), (-1.10, 4.14). At that accuracy the plotted curve at x = 3 reads y = -4.2, and the unlabelled marker at the local minimum reads (3.28, -4.38), whose nearest lattice point is (3, -4), NOT (3, -5). So -5 is not readable off the printed grid; the discrepancy (0.6-0.8 units) is 4-5x the figure's own drafting error. Transcribed exactly as printed per the brief; flagged for the answer-key cross-check pass to adjudicate whether the printed -5 or the drawn figure is wrong. stem: Find the domain and range of \(f(x) = \sqrt{9 - x^2}\).
solution:
\(f(x) = \sqrt{9 - x^2}\) is defined for \(9 - x^2 \ge 0\), i.e. \(x^2 - 9 \le 0\) i.e. \((x - 3)(x + 3) \le 0\)

Therefore \([-3, 3]\) is domain of \(f(x)\). (Verify !)

To find range, let \(\sqrt{9 - x^2} = y\)

Since square root is always positive, so \(y \ge 0\)   ...(I)

Also, on squaring we get \(9 - x^2 = y^2\)

Since, \(-3 \le x \le 3\)

i.e. \(0 \le x^2 \le 9\)

i.e. \(0 \ge -x^2 \ge -9\)

i.e. \(9 \ge 9 - x^2 \ge 9 - 9\)

i.e. \(9 \ge 9 - x^2 \ge 0\)

i.e. \(3 \ge \sqrt{9 - x^2} \ge 0\)

\(\therefore 3 \ge y \ge 0\)   ...(II)

From (I) and (II), \(y \in [0, 3]\) is range of \(f(x)\).
_note: Printed on p-07 (book p.113). The solution marker is the abbreviation 'Soln. :', not 'Solution :'. The solution STRADDLES the column break: it begins in the left column and its last five lines (from 'i.e. 9 >= 9 - x^2 >= 0' through 'From (I) and (II)...') are at the TOP of the right column of the same page. Book wording 'Since square root is always positive' is loose (non-negative is meant, and the book's own next line writes y >= 0); transcribed as printed.

stem: Find domain and range of the function \(f(x) = \frac{6 - 4x^2}{4x + 5}\).
solution:
\(f(x)\) is defined for all \(x \in R\) except when denominator is 0.

Since, \(4x + 5 = 0 \Rightarrow x = -\frac{5}{4}\).

So Domain of \(f(x)\) is \(R - \left\{-\frac{5}{4}\right\}\).

To find the range, let \(y = \frac{6 - 4x^2}{4x + 5}\)

i.e. \(y(4x + 5) = 6 - 4x^2\)

i.e. \(4x^2 + (4y)x + 5y - 6 = 0\).

This is a quadratic equation in \(x\) with \(y\) as constant.

Since \(x \in R - \left\{-\frac{5}{4}\right\}\), i.e. \(x\) is real, we get Solution if, \(D = b^2 - 4ac \ge 0\)

i.e. \((4y)^2 - 4(4)(5y - 6) \ge 0\)

\(16y^2 - 16(5y - 6) \ge 0\)

\(y^2 - 5y + 6 \ge 0\)

\((y - 2)(y - 3) \ge 0\)

Therefore \(y \le 2\) or \(y \ge 3\) (Verify!)

Range of \(f(x)\) is \((-\infty, 2] \cup [3, \infty)\).
_note: Printed on p-08 (book p.114). MID-COLUMN / COLUMN-WISE BOUNDARY: the stem 'Ex. 8 :' is the LAST item in the left column and its entire printed solution sits in the RIGHT column of the same page. This example uses the full marker 'Solution :', unlike Ex. 6 and Ex. 7 on p-07 which use 'Soln. :'. Printed prose carries three spelling/grammar slips, corrected here: 'exccept' -> 'except', 'denominators is 0' -> 'denominator is 0'; the phrase 'we get Solution if, D = b^2 - 4ac >= 0' is printed exactly so (awkward but mathematically intended as 'the equation has a real solution if D >= 0') and is kept verbatim. Mathematics verified independently: D = 16(y^2 - 5y + 6) >= 0 gives y <= 2 or y >= 3, and x = -5/4 is never a root of 4x^2 + 4yx + 5y - 6 = 0 (it evaluates to 1/4), so the excluded point costs the range nothing — the printed range is correct.

The last line of the printed solution reads 'Doamin is [1,2]' - a misprint of 'Domain'; transcribed as 'Domain'. The solution STRADDLES a mid-column boundary: it begins at the foot of the left column of printed p.115 (image p-09) and continues at the top of the right column of the same page.

context: If \(f(x) = \dfrac{2}{x + 5}\) and \(g(x) = x^2 - 1\), then find
solution:
As \((f \circ g)(x) = f[g(x)]\) and \(f(x) = \dfrac{2}{x + 5}\)
Replace \(x\) from \(f(x)\) by \(g(x)\), to get
\((f \circ g)(x) = \dfrac{2}{g(x) + 5}\)
\(= \dfrac{2}{x^2 - 1 + 5}\)
\(= \dfrac{2}{x^2 + 4}\)

solution:
As \((g \circ f)(x) = g[f(x)]\) and \(g(x) = x^2 - 1\)
Replace \(x\) by \(f(x)\), to get
\((g \circ f)(x) = [f(x)]^2 - 1\)
\(= \left(\dfrac{2}{x + 5}\right)^2 - 1\)

stem: If \(f(x) = x^2\), \(g(x) = x + 5\), and \(h(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}\), \(x \ne 0\), find \((g \circ f \circ h)(x)\)
solution:
\((g \circ f \circ h)(x)\)
\(= g\left\{f[h(x)]\right\}\)
\(= g\left[f\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\right]\)
\(= g\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^2\right]\)
\(= \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^2 + 5\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{x^2} + 5\)

stem: Verify that \(f(x) = \dfrac{x - 5}{8}\) and \(g(x) = 8x + 5\) are inverse functions of each other.
solution:
As \(f(x) = \dfrac{x - 5}{8}\), replace \(x\) in \(f(x)\) with \(g(x)\)
\(f[g(x)] = \dfrac{g(x) - 5}{8} = \dfrac{8x + 5 - 5}{8} = \dfrac{8x}{8} = x\)
and \(g(x) = 8x + 5\), replace \(x\) in \(g(x)\) with \(f(x)\)
\(g[f(x)] = 8f(x) + 5 = 8\left[\dfrac{x - 5}{8}\right] + 5 = x - 5 + 5\)
\(= x\)
As \(f[g(x)] = x\) and \(g[f(x)] = x\), \(f\) and \(g\) are inverse functions of each other.

stem: Determine whether the function \(f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}\) has inverse, if it exists find it.
solution:
\(f^{-1}\) exists only if \(f\) is one-one and onto.
Consider \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\),
Therefore,
\(\dfrac{2x_1 + 1}{x_1 - 3} = \dfrac{2x_2 + 1}{x_2 - 3}\)
\((2x_1 + 1)(x_2 - 3) = (2x_2 + 1)(x_1 - 3)\)
\(2x_1x_2 - 6x_1 + x_2 - 3 = 2x_1x_2 - 6x_2 + x_1 - 3\)
\(-6x_1 + x_2 = -6x_2 + x_1\)
\(6x_1 + x_2 = 6x_2 + x_1\)
\(7x_2 = 7x_1\)
\(x_2 = x_1\)
Hence, \(f\) is one-one function.
Let \(f(x) = y\), so \(y = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}\)
Express \(x\) as function of \(y\), as follows
\(y = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}\)
\(y(x - 3) = 2x + 1\)
\(xy - 3y = 2x + 1\)
\(xy - 2x = 3y + 1\)
\(x(y - 2) = 3y + 1\)
\(\therefore\ x = \dfrac{3y + 1}{y - 2}\) for \(y \ne 2\).
Thus for any \(y \ne 2\),
we have \(x\) such that \(f(x) = y\)
\(f^{-1}\) is well defined on \(R - \{2\}\)
If \(f(x) = 2\) i.e. \(2x + 1 = 2(x - 3)\)
i.e. \(2x + 1 = 2x - 6\) i.e. \(1 = -6\)
Which is contradiction.
\(2 \notin\) Range of \(f\).
Here the range of \(f(x)\) is \(R - \{2\}\).
\(x\) is defined for all \(y\) in the range.
Therefore \(f(x)\) is onto function.
As \(f\) is one-one and onto, so \(f^{-1}\) exists.
As \(f(x) = y\), so \(f^{-1}(y) = x\)
Therefore, \(f^{-1}(y) = \dfrac{3y + 1}{y - 2}\)
Replace \(x\) by \(y\), to get
\(f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x + 1}{x - 2}\).
_note: TWO printed defects in the solution, both transcribed as printed. (1) The line \(6x_1 + x_2 = 6x_2 + x_1\) is a subscript misprint: it does NOT follow from the line above it (\(-6x_1 + x_2 = -6x_2 + x_1\)), and the line BELOW it (\(7x_2 = 7x_1\)) does not follow from it either — from \(6x_1 + x_2 = 6x_2 + x_1\) one gets \(5x_1 = 5x_2\), not \(7x_2 = 7x_1\). The intended line is \(6x_2 + x_2 = 6x_1 + x_1\), which does give \(7x_2 = 7x_1\). Verified on the page image at high zoom. The final conclusion \(x_1 = x_2\) is correct either way. (2) The closing instruction reads 'Replace \(x\) by \(y\)' where the step performed is the reverse — replacing \(y\) by \(x\) in \(f^{-1}(y) = \dfrac{3y+1}{y-2}\) to obtain \(f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x+1}{x-2}\). The resulting formula is correct. The printed solution also STRADDLES a page break: it begins on p-16 (right column, ending at \(y(x-3) = 2x+1\)) and continues at the top of the left column of p-17; both pages are inside this band, so the solution is complete.

stem: If \(\{x\}\) and \([x]\) are the fractional part function and greatest integer function of \(x\) respectively, solve for \(x\), if \(\{x+1\}+2x=4[x+1]-6\).
solution:
\(\{x+1\}+2x=4[x+1]-6\)

Since \(\{x+n\}=\{x\}\) and \([x+n]=[x]+n\), for \(n\in I\), also \(x=[x]+\{x\}\)

\(\therefore\;\{x\}+2(\{x\}+[x])=4([x]+1)-6\)

\(\therefore\;\{x\}+2\{x\}+2[x]=4[x]+4-6\)

\(\therefore\;3\{x\}=4[x]-2[x]-2\)

\(\therefore\;3\{x\}=2[x]-2\)  ... (I)

Since \(0\le\{x\}<1\)

\(\therefore\;0\le 3\{x\}<3\)

\(\therefore\;0\le 2[x]-2<3\)  \((\because\) from I\()\)

\(\therefore\;0+2\le 2[x]<3+2\)

\(\therefore\;2\le 2[x]<5\)

\(\therefore\;\frac{2}{2}\le[x]<\frac{5}{2}\)

\(\therefore\;1\le[x]<2.5\)

But as \([x]\) takes only integer values

\([x]=1,2\) since \([x]=1\Rightarrow 1\le x<2\) and \([x]=2\Rightarrow 2\le x<3\)

Therefore \(x\in[1,3)\)
_note:
COLUMN-WISE STRADDLE: stem, "Solution :" and the working down to \(1\le[x]<2.5\) are in the RIGHT column of p-20; the final three lines ("But as \([x]\) takes only integer values" ... "Therefore \(x\in[1,3)\)") continue at the TOP of the LEFT column of p-21. Transcribed whole.
BOOK DEFECT (answer-affecting, concluding lines). Having found \([x]\in\{1,2\}\), the book never substitutes back into its own equation (I) \(3\{x\}=2[x]-2\) to recover \(\{x\}\); it simply unions the two intervals \([x]=1\Rightarrow 1\le x<2\) and \([x]=2\Rightarrow 2\le x<3\) and prints \(x\in[1,3)\). Substituting gives \([x]=1\Rightarrow 3\{x\}=0\Rightarrow\{x\}=0\Rightarrow x=1\), and \([x]=2\Rightarrow 3\{x\}=2\Rightarrow\{x\}=\frac{2}{3}\Rightarrow x=\frac{8}{3}\). So the solution set is \(\{1,\frac{8}{3}\}\), two isolated points, not the interval \([1,3)\) — e.g. \(x=1.5\) lies in the printed answer but gives LHS \(=0.5+3=3.5\) and RHS \(=4(2)-6=2\). Transcribed as printed per the brief.
